Securing communities and funding military/veteran healthcare is essential—but real results require cutting the bloat that siphons taxpayer dollars from core priorities. While Congress pours billions into foreign aid and redundant programs (like USAID’s $3M for Uzbekistan’s cotton industry “transparency”), DOGE’s termination of 5,200 non-essential contracts proves where the real savings lie. 

Redirecting $60M+ from larval fish monitoring and idle software licenses to veterans’ care isn’t just smart—it’s non-negotiable. Transparency isn’t optional: every contract cancellation and grant termination is now public record. 

If we’re serious about “delivering results,” start by torching the waste that undermines American priorities.

@RepMackenzie Representative Mackenzie - thank you for taking the time to host a webinar that is incredibly important to the members of the American Association of Retired Republicans!

Hosting webinars won't fix Social Security's core problem: a 38% budget explosion from $1.1T to $1.5T since 2019 while services stagnate. The real issue? Bureaucrats burned through your payroll taxes to fuel a $1.8T deficit instead of securing retirement funds.

Until we audit every dollar flowing through SSA's bloated bureaucracy, these "informational events" are just taxpayer-funded theater.

Glad Richard’s issue got resolved, but why does a citizen need congressional intervention just to fix basic Social Security errors? The system’s so bloated and broken, people are forced to beg politicians for help navigating bureaucratic mazes.

Medicare’s no better—deductions vanish into administrative black holes while seniors jump through hoops. Real reform means slashing red tape, automating corrections, and holding agencies accountable when they screw up.

Until then, every “success story” like this just highlights how D.C.’s incompetence punishes taxpayers.

Congressman Mackenzie touts 1,238 cases resolved—but why does a single district need FOUR offices to handle basic constituent services? The Allentown HQ plus Bethlehem, Lehighton, and Northampton offices duplicate bureaucracy instead of streamlining it. Veterans deserve efficient support, not redundant administrative bloat.

If agencies like Social Security and Medicare functioned properly, congressional staff wouldn’t need to clean up their mess. Cut the red tape, fund VA reforms, and stop forcing taxpayers to fund multiple offices for problems Washington created.

Efficiency isn’t optional—it’s how you actually honor service.
@RepMackenzie Now you get to vote for or against the very bill that gets rid of all of those protections and programs. We’ll be watching you.

Celebrating heritage is vital, but let’s not ignore the fiscal backdrop. While festivals like Allentown’s showcase community pride, taxpayers foot the bill for federal grants funneled into “cultural initiatives” that often duplicate local efforts.

Case in point: USAID’s $3M “Community Cultural Preservation” program in 2024, which subsidized events already funded by private donors and municipal budgets. Redirect that cash to secure borders, not redundant parades.

Local pride thrives without D.C. slush funds—cut the bloat, let communities self-fund, and prioritize national needs.

Rep. Mackenzie’s bill tackles Medicare Advantage’s bureaucratic maze—where 75% of denied prior auths get overturned anyway. Electronic streamlining? Long overdue. But let’s not pretend insurers will suddenly play fair.

H.R. 3514 forces transparency, but the real fix is gutting the entire prior auth racket. Seniors shouldn’t need Congress to pass a law just to get timely care insurers already promised.

Cut the red tape, audit denials, and claw back every dollar wasted on these delays. Until then, bureaucrats win, patients lose.

Recognizing local efforts to assist seniors with Medicare coverage is commendable, but let’s not ignore the systemic rot in federal healthcare bureaucracy. While Hitcho Insurance provides free consultations to navigate this maze, Medicare itself remains a fiscal disaster—fraudulent billing costs taxpayers $60B annually, and administrative bloat consumes 8% of spending compared to 2% in private insurance.

The real issue? Washington’s refusal to streamline Medicare’s 1,200+ pages of regulations that force agencies like Hitcho to clean up the mess. Redirecting even 10% of Medicare’s $900B budget from paperwork to patient care would do more for seniors than any broker’s Band-Aid.

Efficiency starts with gutting bureaucracy, not applauding those forced to navigate it.

Another feel-good bill that misses the root problem. H.R. 3128 adds layers to the tax code instead of fixing it—diapers shouldn’t need carveouts in a system that already bleeds families dry. The Fair Tax Act (H.R. 25) slashes IRS overreach entirely, letting families keep their paychecks without jumping through HSA hoops.

Prohibiting state diaper taxes? Good. But real reform means abolishing all regressive sales taxes, not micromanaging exemptions.

Simplify the code, don’t expand it.

The Nancy Gardner Sewell Medicare Multi-Cancer Early Detection Screening Coverage Act (S. 339) claims to expand cancer screening but reeks of bureaucratic overreach. Section 2(a) forces Medicare to cover unproven blood tests starting in 2028, locking payment rates to existing stool DNA tests ($641+ per test) without cost controls.

With 70% of cancers already detected in Medicare patients, this risks billions in redundant screenings while Section 2(b)(2) bizarrely restricts testing to those under 68+ (increasing yearly).

Prioritizing speculative tech over proven diagnostics? Classic DC: fund Pharma’s pet projects while underfunding mammograms/colonoscopies that save lives today.
